What it is: The final compiled RFP 9929 packet - preliminary cost estimates, lease rationale, public-bid record, cost comparison, and bid scoring - for the Troy Michigan Works! professional office space lease.

Need: The current lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400 expires October 31, 2021; a 3-5 year lease is needed to maintain the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, serving 17,000+ job seekers and hundreds of area businesses annually.

Market comparison (Signature Associates, no cost): 3221 W. Big Beaver $17.00; 3270 W. Big Beaver $15.50; 2855 Coolidge Hwy $17.50; 2800 Livernois Rd $17.95; 850 Stephenson Hwy $13.00; 700 Tower Dr $17.95-18.95 (all per sq ft, plus electric).

Moving cost estimate: $150,000-$200,000 (technology upgrades, server moves, build-out, packing, furniture).

Public bid: RFP 9929 announced Aug 3, 2021 (newspaper + troy.k12.mi.us), sent to five brokers plus 19 SIGMA VSS/DM contacts. Two proposals received: L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The document is the final compiled request-for-proposal package supporting RFP 9929 - Professional Office Space, the building lease for the Troy location of Oakland County Michigan Works! (OCMW! Troy), presented as consent-agenda item 5.C at the September 21, 2021 regular Board of Education meeting. It combines several sections: Preliminary Lease Cost Estimates, Lease Rationale, RFP/Public Bid record, a Lease Costs comparison, and Scoring of Bids.

Need for a new lease: The district's existing OCMW! Troy lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400, expires October 31, 2021, and a three-to-five-year lease is required to maintain operations of what the packet calls the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, which provides workforce services to more than 17,000 job seekers and hundreds of area businesses each year.

Cost reasonableness: The district engaged Signature Associates, at no cost, to obtain comparable market quotes. The 2021 quotes were: 3221 W. Big Beaver, Troy, $17.00/sq ft; 3270 W. Big Beaver Road, $15.50/sq ft; 2855 Coolidge Hwy, $17.50/sq ft; 2800 Livernois Rd, $17.95/sq ft; 850 Stephenson Hwy, $13.00/sq ft; and 700 Tower Dr, $17.95-18.95/sq ft - each plus electric. Estimated moving costs, should the office relocate, range from $150,000 to $200,000, covering technology upgrades, server moves, new-facility build-out, packing, furniture, and other costs.

Public bid process: RFP 9929 was announced publicly on Tuesday, August 3, 2021 (with a newspaper announcement included in the packet) and posted on the district website, www.troy.k12.mi.us. It was sent directly to five area brokers: Robbins Investments 550 LLC (Rob Krochmal, 248-867-3304); L. Mason Capitani Corfac International (Mason Capitani, 248-637-7795); Winston-Traitel Realty, Inc. (Jeff Raitt, 248-624-7200); Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions (Robert Gagniuk, 248-830-9400); and Thomas Duke Realty (Rachel Pannell, 248-476-3700). The district also used the State of Michigan SIGMA VSS/DM system, adding 19 contacts. Two firms - L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate - submitted proposals by the August 18, 2021 deadline.

Lease cost comparison: L. Mason Capitani proposed 7,494 square feet at $14.00/sq ft in 2021-22 ($104,916.00), rising to $15.25/sq ft in 2025-26 ($114,283.50), with intermediate years of $106,789.50, $110,536.00, and $112,410.00. Friedman Real Estate proposed 7,000-10,000 square feet with a first-year rate of $15.00/sq ft and a stated 2% annual increase, yielding ranges from $105,000-$150,000 (2021-22) to $113,680-$162,400 (2025-26). All bid amounts are plus electric and include daily janitorial service; L. Mason Capitani's costs include common-area maintenance (CAM), while Friedman's CAM is additional.

Scoring of bids: On location and proximity to the client population (50 points), L. Mason Capitani scored 45 and Friedman 40 - Capitani was noted as close to a bus stop and two expressways (I-696 and I-75) serving Troy/Clawson/Madison Heights, while Friedman was close to a bus stop and one expressway (I-75) serving Troy/Rochester Hills. On cost reasonableness (25 points), Capitani scored 25 and Friedman 20. The overall rate-per-square-foot scoring detail is truncated in the extracted text. The packet supports awarding the five-year lease to L. Mason Capitani.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The document sets out the Troy School District's rationale for its RFP 9929 - Professional Office Space lease recommendation for the Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy (OCMW! Troy) office. It explains that the district's current lease at 550 Stephenson Hwy, Suite 400, expires October 31, 2021, and that a three-to-five-year lease is needed to maintain operations of the premier One Stop Service Center in Oakland County, which serves more than 17,000 job seekers and hundreds of area businesses annually.

To establish cost reasonableness, the district used Signature Associates, at no cost, to obtain comparable market quotes for 2021: 3221 W. Big Beaver, Troy, $17.00/sq ft; 3270 W. Big Beaver Road, $15.50/sq ft; 2855 Coolidge Hwy, $17.50/sq ft; 2800 Livernois Rd, $17.95/sq ft; 850 Stephenson Hwy, $13.00/sq ft; and 700 Tower Dr, $17.95-18.95/sq ft - all plus electric. Relocating the office was estimated to cost $150,000-$200,000, including technology upgrades, server moves, new-facility build-out, packing, and furniture.

RFP 9929 was announced publicly on Tuesday, August 3, 2021, with a newspaper announcement and posting on the district website (www.troy.k12.mi.us), and was sent to five area brokers: Robbins Investments 550 LLC (Rob Krochmal, 248-867-3304); L. Mason Capitani Corfac International (Mason Capitani, 248-637-7795); Winston-Traitel Realty, Inc. (Jeff Raitt, 248-624-7200); Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions (Robert Gagniuk, 248-830-9400); and Thomas Duke Realty (Rachel Pannell, 248-476-3700). The State of Michigan SIGMA VSS/DM system added 19 more contacts. L. Mason Capitani and Friedman Real Estate submitted proposals by the August 20, 2021 deadline.

The lease cost comparison shows L. Mason Capitani at 7,494 square feet with annual costs from $104,916.00 (2021-22, $14.00/sq ft) to $114,283.50 (2025-26, $15.25/sq ft), and Friedman Real Estate at 7,000-10,000 square feet with a first-year $15.00/sq ft rate and a 2% annual increase, ranging from $105,000-$150,000 up to $113,680-$162,400. All bid amounts are plus electric and include daily janitorial service; L. Mason Capitani's costs include common-area maintenance (CAM), while Friedman's is additional.

A three-member committee reviewed and scored the proposals: Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor for the Troy School District; Denise Van Hee, Director of Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy; and Cheryl Schubeck, Program Coordinator of Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy. Final scores reflected the average of the three reviewers' scores in each category. All three scored L. Mason Capitani at 45/25/25 and Friedman Real Estate at 40/20/25. Based on the scoring, the district determined that L. Mason Capitani's proposal was the most reasonable and cost-effective option, noting its rate per square foot is below current market rates and that relocating would be very costly. The rationale therefore supports awarding the lease to L. Mason Capitani.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The document is the suggested Board of Education resolution for Curriculum consideration item 7.B at the regular meeting of September 21, 2021, titled 'CONSIDERATION: Approval of Strategic Plan 2021-2026.'

It opens with context: in the 2015-2016 school year, the Troy School Board of Education joined with the Superintendent and his team to introduce the District's 'Vision of World Class 2020,' and the resulting Strategic Plan 'Pillars' guided the work across oneTROY for the prior five years. The document states that best practice suggests it is appropriate to revisit the District's goals and engage in a collaborative process to reimagine the next Strategic Plan.

The recommended action is to accept the resolution. The suggested resolution's WHEREAS clauses recount the planning process: the Troy School District engaged in a strategic planning process over the past year to create the 2021-2026 Strategic Plan; the process included information-gathering interviews with key stakeholders, including the Board of Education, Central Office administration, building administrators, teachers, professional and support staff, students, parents, and community members. On March 13, 2021, the Board held a strategic planning session during a winter retreat, providing a structured forum to evaluate the output of the information-gathering process and give input on the initial draft. Through an additional workshop on May 4, 2021, the Board addressed key issues, clarified directions and priorities, and provided input and recommendations to inform the plan's development. With input received during a September 7, 2021 workshop, a final draft of the Strategic Plan was produced.

The operative clause resolves that the Troy Board of Education approves, substantially in the form presented to the Board at the meeting, the Strategic Plan 2021-2026, as adopted on the 21st day of September 2021 by the Troy Board of Education. The document includes standard procedural fields for 'Moved by,' 'Supported by,' and the 'Yes'/'No' vote tally, which are blank in the extracted text. This item is paired with the informational report presented under item 7.A by Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction. The extracted text does not include the substantive content of the plan itself - its goals, pillars, or measures - only the approving resolution and its procedural history.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The presentation, 'Troy School District Capital Projects Update, September 2021,' was delivered to the Board of Education as item 8.A and summarizes the district's 2021 facilities and capital work. Its headline figure is that more than $5 million of projects were completed throughout the District during the year.

The work is organized by category. Concrete was added or replaced at various sites, with slides highlighting IAE, Larson, and Costello. Door and window replacement was completed at Hamilton and Wass elementary schools. Fencing was added or replaced districtwide as needed, including at AHS and Leonard. Flooring and polishing work at Costello, Martell, Leonard, Morse, Troy Union, and Smith included approximately 100,000 square feet of flooring replaced and about 2 miles of rubber base replaced; these flooring replacements are labeled 'BSSF.' Paving projects were completed at Bemis, Costello, Wattles, Larson, the Transportation site, and Troy High. Remodeling took place at Smith Middle School and Troy High School. Roofing was replaced at Leonard, Martell, Troy Union, Smith, and Troy High, totaling 152,000 square feet - described as roughly 10% of the approximately 1.7 million square feet of roof in the district.

A substantial portion of the deck consists of before-and-after photographs documenting the work. Featured projects include the Troy High School Media Center remodeling (multiple before/after slides), the Smith Middle School stage remodeling, and the Hamilton and Wass window replacement. Additional slides show the Bemis and Wattles paving, the Troy High and Transportation paving (including a Troy Union 'before' view), BSSF flooring replacements at Leonard and Morse, roof replacements at Smith Middle and Troy Union (with Leonard and Martell before/after comparisons), polishing projects at Costello, Leonard, Martell, Morse, and Troy Union (with Troy Union and Martell examples), and fencing and concrete additions and replacements districtwide.

The presentation is informational and accompanies the district's Business report on 2013 Bond and Sinking Fund work at the September 21, 2021 regular meeting. It does not itemize per-project dollar amounts beyond the aggregate figure of more than $5 million, but it quantifies scope through the square-footage figures for flooring (100,000 sq ft) and roofing (152,000 sq ft) and the two miles of rubber base. The named schools and sites - including Troy High, Smith Middle, Costello, Leonard, Martell, Morse, Troy Union, Bemis, Wattles, Larson, Hamilton, Wass, and the Transportation facility - indicate the districtwide scope of the 2021 capital program funded through bond and sinking-fund resources.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Character.org, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit and national advocate for character development, issued this press release on May 11, 2021 certifying 47 schools and one district as 2021 National Schools of Character, along with schools in Brazil (CEL Intercultural School, Rio de Janeiro) and Mexico (Escuela Secundaria Tecnológico de Monterrey Zacatecas, Guadalupe). The release appears in the Troy School District Board of Education’s September 21, 2021 regular meeting materials because two district schools earned the honor. In Michigan, the certified schools were Bemis Elementary School (Troy), Hart Middle School (Rochester), and Troy Union Elementary School (Troy).

Dr. Arthur Schwartz, President of Character.org, is quoted saying the educators at these schools “model and reinforce the core values of respect and dignity” and teach students “to be honest and trustworthy, to contribute their time and talents to the common good, and when necessary, to show the courage to stand up for what is right.” Lori Soifer, who directs the Schools of Character program (press contact lori@character.org), noted the schools completed the application and review process “in a year that has been anything but typical.”

Certification requires meeting the rigorous standards of Character.org’s 11 Principles Framework for Schools, with each school assessed by a team of trained evaluators. Since the program’s inception it has impacted over 3 million students, staff, parents, and community members. The 2021 honorees were to be recognized at Character.org’s Annual Forum, held virtually October 20-22, 2021.

Other honorees named across states included Vestavia Hills Elementary West (Alabama); Brentwood Lower School, Los Angeles (California); Orlando Science Elementary School and Seminole Middle School (Florida); Thomas W. Pyle Middle School, Bethesda (Maryland); numerous Missouri schools such as Bayless High School and Busch Middle School of Character (St. Louis); a large New Jersey contingent including Cherry Hill East High School and the district-level Rockaway Township Schools (denoted a District of Character); Pelham Middle School and St. HOPE Leadership Academy (New York); Union Academy Charter School (North Carolina); Jefferson Elementary School, Pryor (Oklahoma); Pennsbury High School (Pennsylvania); and several Texas Harmony Science Academy and School of Science and Technology campuses.

About Character.org: founded in 1993, the nonprofit provides voice, visibility, and resources for educators to build nurturing, supportive school cultures focused on core values and character strengths. Over the past 20 years, more than 1,000 schools and school districts have been certified as National Schools of Character after independent, rigorous evaluation. The organization is widely known for its 11 Principles framework, developed by school leaders and character-development researchers, and envisions expanding its work to families, sports, and the workplace.

The engagement was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, obligating the auditors to communicate matters such as compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements, instances of error or fraud, illegal acts, and significant deficiencies in internal control; a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 addresses internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing.

Under Significant Audit Findings and the Qualitative Aspects of Accounting Practices, the auditors report that no new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies did not change during 2021; that they noted no transactions lacking authoritative guidance or consensus; and no significant transactions recognized in a period different from when they occurred. They identify the most sensitive accounting estimates as the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other post-employment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A Facilities Condition and Program Assessment Report prepared for Troy School District and presented to the Board of Education at the October 5, 2021 Workshop. The work was organized around two areas of focus: a Facilities Condition Assessment of interior and exterior infrastructure and sites against code and standards (using condition categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+ years), and a Program Assessment identifying barriers and deficiencies in school buildings and sites that impede delivering education optimally now and in the future.

Process and scale: the effort began with a kick-off meeting in March 2021, followed by facility tours from March through August 2021, status meetings, project worklists, quantification of items, cost estimates, and categorization/prioritization. Reported scale statistics include roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings (more than 50 acres), approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures, over 4,300 doors, over 2 million square feet of parking lot, 1.7 million square feet of roofing, an average building age of 48 years, and approximately 500 acres of property (about 2.3% of Troy's total area).

Facility findings by system, each with a cost range: Roofing noted aging roofs against a typical 20-year lifespan, $10-15 million; Architectural Systems (aging doors, flooring, furnishings such as cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards), $40-45 million; Mechanical Systems (aging boilers, classroom unit ventilators, malfunctioning plumbing; 20-year equipment lifespan), $45-50 million; Electrical Systems (upgrade lighting to energy-efficient LED, replace emergency/exit lighting, with energy rebates and operational savings; an example cited Troy High School Media Center lighting), $30-35 million; Site Work paving (aging parking lots and sidewalks; 20-year asphalt lifespan), $20-23 million; and Site Work playgrounds/athletics (assessed on condition, age appropriateness, and safety), $5-7 million.

The consolidated Cost Summary by category totals $220-250 million: Roofing Systems $10-15M, Architectural Systems $40-45M, Mechanical Systems $45-50M, Electrical Systems $30-35M, Site Work $25-30M, Furniture and Kitchen Equipment $23-28M, Buses $12M, and Technology Devices $35M. The Cost Summary by priority also totals $220-250 million: Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55M, Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100M, and Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95M.

The Program Assessment portion is not accompanied by a dollar amount, as costs come later in design work. It describes an interplay between facilities needs and program needs, where a program decision such as designing a new instructional space can simultaneously address facilities needs like lighting and architectural upgrades. Its approach covers vision setting and discovery, understanding TSD's vision and goals, defining an ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against that ideal future program of spaces. Feedback gathered from the Board, cabinet, and instructional leaders referenced themes such as making thinking visible, the 6 C's of Learning (Collaboration, Communication, Critical Thinking, Creativity, Character/Compassion, Citizenship), project-based and experiential learning, social-emotional learning, competency-based and mastery learning, and a whole-child multi-tiered system of supports. Teacher input identified top instructional practices (team collaborative work, one-on-one with teacher, learning with mobile technology, project-based learning) and attributes of spaces that draw teachers, including good lighting, natural light, clean and decluttered rooms, and flexibility to change the space.

A recognition item, styled a "TSD Mission Moment," prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting of October 19, 2021 (agenda item 2.A). It honors Hill Elementary School's schoolwide "Color Run."

Hill Elementary students participated in the Color Run event on Friday, October 1st. The write-up explains that this Fun Run was specifically designed to be inclusive and mindful of students who might have sensory issues. A Color Run involves colorful chalk being thrown into the air and decorating the shirts of those running by, and Fun Runs typically involve lots of cheering, music, loud audio, and visual stimulants. For a portion of Hill's Color Run, the music was turned off and cheering consisted of hands in the air and thumbs up instead of clapping and raised voices. The quiet allowed students who have sensory issues to fully enjoy the run, while the entire fifth grade was present to quietly but enthusiastically cheer participants on. The narrative emphasizes that the reduced volume and stimulation did not diminish the joy of participants, and frames the event as an example of the District's Red Pillar (Equity & Well-Being) at its finest, reinforcing the message that "ALL means ALL in the TSD."

The recommended action is to invite Shari Pawlus to introduce the Hill parents who organized the event: Nikki Bengry, Stacy Glass, Britney McIntyre, and Kelly Madden.

It is organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4) and Informational Items (pages 5-15).

Auditor and key dates:
- Independent auditors: Plante & Moran, PLLC
- Engagement letter dated June 2, 2021; audit-planning meeting held August 13, 2021
- Audit report and this communication dated October 5, 2021; fiscal year ended June 30, 2021

Key points:
- The audit gives reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the financial statements are free of material misstatement and fairly presented in conformity with U.S. GAAP; it does not relieve management of its responsibilities.
- Internal control was considered only to design audit procedures, not to express an opinion on its effectiveness.
- A separate letter dated October 5, 2021 addresses internal control over financial reporting and compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements under Government Auditing Standards.
- No new accounting policies were adopted and existing policies were applied unchanged during 2021; no transactions were noted that lacked authoritative guidance or that were recognized in a different period than they occurred.
- The most sensitive accounting estimates are the district's proportionate shares of the MPSERS net pension liability and net OPEB liability (GASB Statements 68 and 75).

Acknowledgments: The auditors thank Assistant Superintendent Rick West, Director of Finance Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their preparedness and assistance.

Purpose: Presented under agenda item 8.B in support of the Board's acceptance of the 2020-2021 audit.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Overview: Plante & Moran, PLLC's "Report to the Board of Education" for Troy School District, delivered together with the audit of the district's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021. This is the auditor-to-governance communication required by U.S. professional standards (AU-C 260) and is distinct from the audit opinion itself. The report is dated October 5, 2021 and is organized into two parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4) and Informational Items (pages 5-15).

Responsibilities and scope: As stated in the engagement letter dated June 2, 2021, the auditors' responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management, with the Board's oversight, are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit provides reasonable, but not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement and does not relieve the Board or management of their responsibilities. As part of the audit, the firm considered the district's internal control solely to design appropriate audit procedures, not to opine on the effectiveness of that control. The audit was performed according to the scope and timing communicated at a planning meeting on August 13, 2021.

Government Auditing Standards: Because the audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, the auditors are obligated to communicate certain matters -- including compliance with provisions of laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements; instances of error or fraud; illegal acts applicable to government agencies; and significant deficiencies in internal control. To that end, a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 was issued regarding the auditors' consideration of internal control over financial reporting and their tests of compliance.

Significant audit findings: Management is responsible for the selection and use of appropriate accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. The report states that no new accounting policies were adopted and that the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. The auditors noted no transactions entered into by the district for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in a different period than when they occurred.

Sensitive estimates: Accounting estimates are described as an integral part of the financial statements, based on management's knowledge and assumptions about future events. The most sensitive estimates affecting the statements were the district's share of the Michigan Public School Employees' Retirement System (MPSERS) net liabilities for the pension plan and the other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plan, recorded on the government-wide statements pursuant to GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, respectively.

Acknowledgments and use: The auditors express gratitude to Mr. Rick West (Assistant Superintendent, Business Services), Ms. Kandice Moynihan (Director of Finance), and the business office for their assistance and preparedness, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities. The document appears under agenda item 8.B of the October 19, 2021 regular Board meeting as part of the package supporting the Board's acceptance of the fiscal year 2021 audit.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Overview: Troy School District's Federal Awards Supplemental Information as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021. This is the "single audit" reporting package required under the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR Part 200) for entities that expend federal awards, and it is issued under separate cover from the district's Annual Comprehensive Financial Report. It appears in the fiscal year 2021 audit package presented under agenda item 8.B of the October 19, 2021 regular Board meeting.

Table of contents: The package comprises the independent auditor's Report on the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards Required by the Uniform Guidance (page 1); the Report on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting and on Compliance and Other Matters Based on an Audit of Financial Statements Performed in Accordance with Government Auditing Standards (pages 2-3); the Report on Compliance for Each Major Federal Program and Report on Internal Control Over Compliance Required by the Uniform Guidance (pages 4-5); the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (pages 6-9); the Reconciliation of Basic Financial Statements Federal Revenue with the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (page 10); the Notes to the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (page 11); and the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs (page 12).

Relationship to the financial statements: The auditors state that they audited the financial statements of the governmental activities, each major fund, and the aggregate remaining fund information of the district as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021, together with the related notes, which collectively comprise the basic financial statements, and that they issued their report thereon dated October 5, 2021 containing an unmodified opinion. They note that no procedures were performed with respect to the audited financial statements subsequent to October 5, 2021.

Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards: The accompanying Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards and the reconciliation of basic financial statements federal revenue with that schedule are presented for purposes of additional analysis as required by the Uniform Guidance and are not a required part of the basic financial statements. The information is the responsibility of management and was derived from and relates directly to the underlying accounting and other records used to prepare the financial statements. It was subjected to the auditing procedures applied in the audit of the financial statements and certain additional procedures, including comparing and reconciling the information to the underlying records or to the financial statements. In the auditors' opinion, the information is fairly stated, in all material respects, in relation to the financial statements as a whole.

Internal control and compliance: The internal-control report explains that, in planning and performing the audit, the auditors considered the district's internal control over financial reporting to design appropriate audit procedures, but not to express an opinion on the effectiveness of that internal control; accordingly, no such opinion is expressed. The report defines a deficiency in internal control (when the design or operation of a control does not allow management or employees, in the normal course of their functions, to prevent, or detect and correct, misstatements on a timely basis), a material weakness (a deficiency or combination of deficiencies creating a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement would not be prevented or timely detected and corrected), and a significant deficiency (less severe than a material weakness but important enough to merit attention by those charged with governance). The auditors note that their consideration of internal control was for the limited purpose described and was not designed to identify all deficiencies that might be material weaknesses or significant deficiencies. In the portion of the report shown, they state that during the audit they did not identify any deficiencies in internal control (the excerpt is truncated at this point).

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Overview: A transmittal letter dated October 5, 2021 from Plante & Moran, PLLC to Ms. Kandice Moynihan of Troy School District (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098). The letter accompanies the district's annual financial reports for the year ended June 30, 2021 and serves primarily to summarize the various agencies' filing and distribution requirements so the district can meet them.

Enclosures: The letter encloses the annual financial reports and Report to the Board of Education as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021, specifically the financial statements, the single audit report, and the Report to the Board of Education. It advises that, in general, the financial statements should be included with any distribution of the single audit report, and it defines the "single audit report package" as the financial statements, the single audit report, and the Report to the Board of Education.

Single audit (federal) filing requirements: Plante & Moran states that it is in the process of preparing the data collection form on the district's behalf and will upload the entire reporting package electronically to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse (FAC), so the district no longer needs to send hard copies to the clearinghouse. The district will, however, need to electronically certify the single audit data collection form; it will receive an automated email from the clearinghouse with certification instructions, and the certifying official must set up a personal account within the Internet Data Entry System (IDES) used by the FAC for these filings.

State filing requirements for school districts: One copy of the financial statements, single audit report, and Report to the Board of Education will be transmitted to the Michigan Department of Education on the district's behalf, and Plante & Moran will notify the Department once the data collection form has been submitted. In addition, one copy of the financial statements, single audit report, Report to the Board of Education, and the data collection form (which can be printed from the FAC website) should be forwarded to the intermediate school district by November 1.

Securities and Exchange Commission / continuing disclosure: Because the district has issued bonds after July 1, 1995, it may be required to submit information, including its annual financial statements, to the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board (MSRB); submissions must be made electronically in PDF format to the Electronic Municipal Market Access (EMMA) system (www.emma.msrb.org). The district may also be obligated to provide continuing disclosure documents to a State Information Depository (SID) if required by applicable state law or by a continuing disclosure agreement in effect prior to July 1, 2009. The SID for Michigan is identified as the Municipal Advisory Council of Michigan, Buhl Building, 535 Griswold, Suite 1850, Detroit, MI 48226-3699.

Additional nonfinancial disclosures: The letter cautions that the district's bond documents (either the bond awarding resolution or the bond official statement) may have committed it to additional nonfinancial disclosures such as population, taxable valuation, millage rates, and other demographic data, which may need to be sent to the same repositories -- often with a due date 180 days after year end. The district is advised to contact its bond financial advisors and bond counsel to determine whether these disclosure requirements apply and to obtain assistance in supplying the appropriate information. The letter closes by thanking the district for the opportunity to serve as its auditors and is signed by Plante & Moran, PLLC. It is part of the fiscal year 2021 audit package presented under agenda item 8.B.

The change and its effect: The amendment reduces the current levy on Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest, and Industrial Personal Properties from 4.4575 mills to 3.3878 mills, and increases the Non-Homestead levy from 13.5425 mills to 14.6122 mills, for general operating purposes for the 2021-22 school year. The total levy for the two millage rates combined remains unchanged at 18 mills.

Background (whereas clauses): The Board of Education, pursuant to a 2021-22 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted June 15, 2021, had approved the district's operating, debt, and sinking fund millage rates for the year, including authority to levy 4.4575 mills on Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest, and Industrial Personal Properties and 13.5425 mills on all Non-Homestead Properties, for a total of 18 mills. The FY22 State School Aid Act, 2021 PA 48 (HB 4411), reduces the amount of hold-harmless (OPR ALL) millage that districts may levy in 2021 for FY22. Under Section 1211 of the state school code, per-pupil hold-harmless revenue is limited to the difference between the district's foundation allowance and $8,700, and the Board desires to comply with Section 1211 of the FY22 act.

Resolved clauses: The Board resolves to approve an amendment to the 2021-22 Budget Appropriations Resolution authorizing the district to modify the Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest, and Industrial Personal Properties and the Non-Homestead Properties millage rate levies for a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. It further resolves to authorize the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2021 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) reflecting a Principal Residence/Qualified Agriculture/Qualified Forest/Industrial Personal Properties millage request of 3.3878 mills, with 1.1591 of the 3.3878 mills to be levied on the December 1, 2021 levy date, and a Non-Homestead operating millage request of 14.6122 mills, with 7.8409 of the 14.6122 mills to be levied on the December 1, 2021 levy date. The amended Tax Rate Request is to be submitted to the Oakland County Clerk and the City of Troy Clerk.

Vote and certification: The resolution provides blank "YES" and "NO" member lines and states "RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED." It is certified by Gary Hauff, Secretary of the Board of Education, who attests that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted at a regular meeting and that notice was given under the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended. Notably, the certification block within the document references a regular meeting held November 20, 2018 -- a date that, together with the file name ("11 13 18"), appears to be boilerplate carried over from a prior template rather than the operative October 19, 2021 meeting at which this 2021-22 amendment is being considered.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Email from Assistant Superintendent Rick West (October 5, 2021) informing the Troy School District Board that the FY22 State School Aid Act - 2021 PA 48 (HB 4411) - requires the district to cut its hold-harmless (OPR ALL) winter tax levy from 2.2288 to 1.1591 mills, with the offsetting OPR non-homestead (OPR NH) rate rising from 6.7712 to 7.8409. A revised Form L-4029 was placed on the October 19, 2021 consent agenda; the law raises Troy's foundation allowance by 1.23% ($9,430).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
An October 5, 2021 email from Rick West (Assistant Superintendent, Business Services) to Superintendent Richard Machesky and Judy Holmes (cc Donna Havrilla, Kandice Moynihan), forwarded to the Board, explaining a state-mandated change to the district's 2021 winter tax levy. It transmits a revised Form L-4029 (Tax Rate Request).

The requirement
Under the FY22 State School Aid Act (2021 PA 48, House Bill 4411), hold-harmless districts must reduce the hold-harmless millage they may levy. Troy must lower its hold-harmless (OPR ALL) winter levy from 2.2288 to 1.1591 mills. Correspondingly, the OPR non-homestead (OPR NH) rate increases from 6.7712 to 7.8409 mills. All other millage rates are unchanged.

Financial impacts on Troy
- FY22 foundation allowance increased 1.23% (2020 US CPI) above FY21: +$9,430
- Sec. 20m payment (difference between $171 and the foundation increase): +$56
- Combined local revenue (18 mills) plus state aid funds the first $8,700 of the allowance
- Sec. 1211 hold-harmless per-pupil revenue capped at the difference between the allowance and $8,700: $786
- Total (foundation + 20m + hold harmless): $8,700 + $56 + $786 = $9,486

Next steps
The item was to be discussed briefly under 'other' at the October 5 workshop, with the revised L-4029 placed on the October 19, 2021 consent agenda.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
An internal email dated Tuesday, October 5, 2021 (10:33 a.m.) from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, addressed to Superintendent Richard Machesky and Judy Holmes, with copies to Donna Havrilla and Kandice Moynihan, requesting that the message be forwarded to the Board of Education. The email explains a legally required adjustment to Troy School District's 2021 property-tax levy and transmits a revised Form L-4029 (the 2021 September Revised Tax Rate Request, a two-page attachment).

The substance concerns 'hold-harmless' millage. West explains that the FY22 State School Aid Act - 2021 Public Act 48, House Bill 4411 - reduces the amount of hold-harmless (labeled 'OPR ALL') millage that hold-harmless districts may levy in 2021 for fiscal year 2022. To comply, Troy must reduce its hold-harmless (OPR ALL) winter tax levy from 2.2288 mills to 1.1591 mills. As a mechanical consequence, the district's OPR non-homestead ('OPR NH') rate increases from 6.7712 mills to 7.8409 mills. All other millage rates remain unchanged.

The email itemizes the act's specific provisions and their dollar impact on Troy:
1. The act increases hold-harmless districts' FY22 foundation allowance by 1.23% - the U.S. CPI increase for calendar year 2020 - above the FY21 foundation allowance; Troy's impact is $9,430.
2. The difference between $171 and the dollar increase in the FY22 foundation allowance is paid to districts under Section 20m; Troy's impact is $56.
3. Combined local revenue (18 mills) and state aid pay the first $8,700 of the foundation allowance.
4. Under Section 1211 of the State School Code, per-pupil hold-harmless revenue is limited to the difference between the district's foundation allowance and $8,700; Troy's impact is $786.

West sums these components - foundation allowance plus Section 20m plus hold harmless - as $8,700 + $56 + $786 = $9,486.

Procedurally, West notes the district would briefly discuss this at that evening's workshop under 'other' and would place the revised L-4029 on the October 19th consent agenda for Board action. He invites questions and includes his contact information: Troy School District, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248-823-4022, fax 248-823-4013, email rwest@troy.k12.mi.us. The signature block carries the Central Office tagline about providing outstanding professional service to support teaching and learning for the OneTroy community. The document is significant because it records both the statutory basis (2021 PA 48 / HB 4411) and the exact millage-rate changes and per-pupil funding figures behind Troy's 2021 winter tax levy.

A draft ("D R A F T") Pupil Enrollment Projection Study Report for the years 2022-2026, prepared by PMC (branded pmcresa.com) and presented to the Troy School District on November 9, 2021. The document runs 40 pages and functions as the formal written study accompanying the same-evening PEPS slide presentation to the Board of Education Workshop.

The boundary map (Section 1a) is reproduced across several pages and, in the extracted text, appears as an OCR list of Troy-area street names within the district's attendance boundaries (for example Woodward, Livernois, Rochester, Big Beaver-area residential streets, and interstate I-75). Because the extracted content is dominated by this map OCR, the specific numeric findings - median householder age, family and household counts, birth-cohort survival ratios, and the year-by-year projected K-12 enrollment - are documented in the companion "Troy School District PEPS Presentation 11-09-2021," rather than being legible in this file's extracted text.

The study's purpose is to give the Board reliable multi-year enrollment forecasts, built from GIS/US Census data and cohort-survival methodology, to inform decisions about facilities, staffing, and budgeting. As a draft, it was presented for review at the workshop stage.

The presentation slides for the Troy School District Pupil Enrollment Projection Study (PEPS), delivered to the Board of Education Workshop on November 9, 2021 by PMC. The agenda covered district demographics and trends, pupil enrollment methodology, the district-wide pupil enrollment projection, key takeaways, and questions/answers.

Methodology: PMC's process draws on demographic growth analysis, GIS, US Census Bureau data, and Core Base Statistical Area definitions, comparing a primary area (the district) against Comparison #1 (the county) and Comparison #2 (the state). Projections use the Cohort Survival method associated with Michigan form DS 4061.

Current district demographics: median age of householder 55.1; total number of families 18,603; households with school-age children 11,233; percentage of households with children 43.9%; enrolled school-aged children 12,430. Preschool enrollment splits 43.47% public / 56.53% private, and K-12 enrollment splits 89.54% public / 10.46% private. In the sample projection slide, birth year 2016 shows 13,627 births, a kindergarten percentage of births of 5.31%, K-12 enrollment of 12,196, a difference of 23 students, 0.19% growth, and a total of 12,771.

The "Key Takeaways" compare 2018 to 2020/2021 values. Median householder age rose from 53.4 to 55.1 (+1.7 years). Total housing units went from 26,906 to 27,150. Total families rose from 18,583 to 18,603 (+20). Households with school-age children fell from 11,603 to 11,233 (-370). Enrolled school-aged children fell from 13,017 to 12,430 (-587). Public PK enrollment moved from 43.24% to 43.47%, and private PK from 56.76% to 56.53%. The share of county births enrolled in kindergarten fell from 6.23% to 5.31% (2021), a 0.92% decrease. Total TSD K-12 enrollment declined from 12,548 (2018) to 12,196 (2021), a loss of 352 pupils.

A peer-district comparison shows K-12 enrollment declines from 2018 to 2020 across neighboring systems: Birmingham Public Schools 7,384 to 6,799 (-585); Bloomfield Hills Schools 5,275 to 5,131 (-144); Novi Community Schools 6,711 to 6,596 (-115); Rochester Community Schools 15,412 to 14,987 (-425); Plymouth-Canton Schools 17,303 to 16,598 (-705); and Utica Community Schools 26,599 to 25,672 (-927). Collectively, the data frame Troy's enrollment decline within a regional trend of shrinking, aging households and falling birth-cohort enrollment.

It recommends amending Section 1002/1000.02 to require not less than 24 hours' notice for special Board meetings, aligning with Michigan's Open Meetings Act (MCL 15.261 et seq.), and updating the Student Bullying subpolicy (Policy 2006/2000.06) to comply with MCL 380.1310b, adding detailed definitions, reporting, and implementation requirements for bullying and cyberbullying.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: A memorandum (Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, to Superintendent Rich Machesky; CC Judy Holmes; dated November 4, 2021) transmitting policy changes recommended by Administration and the Policy Committee for Board approval (agenda item 5.D).

Policy changes recommended:

1. Section 1002/1000.02 — Special Meetings
- Adds that special meetings called by the President or any three Board members must provide not less than 24 hours' notice to all Board members.
- Notice to members and the public must follow the Michigan Open Meetings Act (MCL 15.261 et seq.).

2. Policy 2006/2000.06 — Student Bullying (to comply with MCL 380.1310b)
- Prohibits bullying and cyberbullying 'at school' plus off-campus conduct likely to cause substantial disruption.
- Protects all students regardless of subject matter or motivation; bars retaliation and false accusations; keeps a reporter's identity confidential.
- Assigns each building principal responsibility for implementation.
- Requires revising the Student Code of Conduct, posting the policy on the district website, and annual reporting to the Board of all verified bullying incidents and consequences.
- Directs administrative regulations covering reporting, prompt investigation, parent/guardian notification, confidentiality, and documentation.
- Defines 'bullying' (physical, verbal, psychological) and 'at school.'

Purpose: Bring district policy into compliance with Michigan law — the Open Meetings Act and the anti-bullying statute.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum on the Business Office letterhead (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098) from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, to Dr. Rich Machesky, Superintendent of Schools, copied to Judy Holmes, dated Thursday, November 4, 2021, transmitting policy additions and changes recommended by Administration and the Policy Committee for Board of Education approval. The item appeared as agenda item 5.D at the November 16, 2021 regular meeting.

Two policy revisions are recommended. First, an underlined change to Section 1002/1000.02 to ensure compliance with Michigan's Open Meetings Act (MCL 15.261, et seq.). The revised 'Special Meetings' language provides that special meetings of the Board may be called by the President or any three Board members by providing not less than 24 hours' notice to all Board members, with notice to members and the public consistent in manner and form with the requirements of the OMA. (The source shows the notice period being revised, replacing the prior figure.)

Second, underlined changes to the 'Student Bullying' subpolicy, typically found under Policy 2006/2000.06, to comply with MCL 380.1310b. The revised policy states that the Board recognizes bullying and cyberbullying significantly interfere with learning and prohibits bullying 'at school,' as well as off-campus conduct that could likely lead to a material or substantial disruption of the school learning environment. It is intended to protect all students regardless of the subject matter or motivation for the behavior, and it prohibits retaliation or false accusations against a target, witness, or other person with reliable information; the identity of a person who reports bullying is to remain confidential.

The implementation provisions direct that: the principal of each school building is the responsible official for implementing the policy in that building; the Superintendent shall revise the district's Student Code of Conduct to specifically prohibit bullying and cyberbullying and shall post the policy on the district website; and the Superintendent shall report to the Board annually all verified incidents of bullying and the resulting consequences imposed. The Superintendent must promulgate administrative regulations that include a procedure to report an act of bullying, a procedure for prompt investigation by the building principal or designee, notification to the parent or guardian of both the claimed victim and the alleged perpetrator, protection of the confidentiality of a reporter, documentation of any reported incident, and the annual reporting procedure to the Board.

The policy defines 'bullying' as any written, verbal, or physical act or electronic communication (including cyberbullying) intended or reasonably known to be likely to harm one or more district students by substantially interfering with educational opportunities, benefits, or programs; adversely affecting a student's ability to participate by placing them in reasonable fear of physical harm or causing substantial emotional distress; having an actual and substantial detrimental effect on a student's physical or mental health; or causing substantial disruption or interference with the orderly operation of the school. Examples span physical acts (hitting, kicking, pushing, extortion, unwelcome contact), verbal acts (taunting, malicious teasing, threats, gossip), and psychological acts (spreading rumors, manipulating social relationships, coercion, social exclusion, intimidation). 'At school' is defined to include a classroom, anywhere on school premises, a school bus or other school-related vehicle, and school-sponsored activities or events on or off premises, as well as off-premises use of a district-owned or controlled telecommunications device or service.

A principal difference among the bids is the engine. Hoekstra's configuration specifies a Detroit Diesel DD8 260-hp engine with an Allison 3000 transmission (option C211), which the report marks N/A for the other two dealers, while Holland and Midwest Transit are configured with a Cummins ISB 260-hp engine with PTS3000 transmission (option C205).

Representative chassis options include a 240-amp Leece-Neville alternator, a 23,000-lb minimum rear axle, three 12-volt 950-CCA batteries, brake dust shields, and a telescoping steering wheel — standard on Hoekstra and Holland but priced by Midwest Transit ($139, $325, $227, $43, $225 respectively). Adjustable brake and accelerator pedals (C310) cost $332 on Hoekstra and $838 on Holland but are marked N/A for Midwest Transit.

Body options include an all-light monitor system, a battery cut-off switch, an air crossing gate arm with magnet ($300 Hoekstra / $401 Holland / N/A Midwest), increasing emergency exit windows from two to four, an auxiliary ProHeat X45 45,000-BTU quartz-timer heater ($3,420 / $3,582 / $3,200), an 80,000-BTU mid-body rear heater, a perforated-ceiling noise-reduction system ($469 / $629 / S/E), white polyurethane roof paint, an AM/FM radio with CD, clock and interior/exterior PA ($502 / $510 / N/A), a National air-ride driver's seat, gray passenger seats, pebble-tread step tread, air LED stop-arm signals (credits of $314 / $529 / $282), and a luggage passthrough storage compartment with lights, gas spring and lock ($1,968 / $4,250 / $2,120). Deleting the fire-block seat option shows credits of $576 (Hoekstra) and $760 (Midwest).

Listed dealer options include a high-strength (110,000 KSI) chassis frame rail, Zonar V3 hardware, Michelin 11R 16-ply X Multi D rear mud/snow tires ($506), and a back-up camera ($668). Overall, Midwest Transit is the lowest grand total and Holland the highest, but the accompanying district recommendation favors Hoekstra because its specification — notably the Detroit Diesel DD8 engine and other required features — matches the district's requirements.

Strategic themes and schedule

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Business Services Update presented at the Troy School District Board of Education Workshop on December 7, 2021, agenda item 2.A, covering the 2021-22 General Fund Budget Amendment #1, non-recurring/one-time revenue, and the budget schedule.

Revenue adjustments. Local revenue is decreased by approximately $3.1 million, or 7.5 percent: the FY22 State School Aid Act reduced the amount of hold-harmless property-tax millage the district may levy by $248 per pupil, a roughly $3.4 million reduction. State revenue is increased by about $3.4 million, or 3.23 percent, reflecting a Proposal A obligation and discretionary payment increase of $900,000, a foundation allowance of $9,430 (a $115 per-pupil increase) at a projected 12,450 FTE, Section 20m funding of $56 per pupil, and a Section 147c retirement-funding increase of $2.3 million. Federal revenue is increased by about $1.0 million, or 16.7 percent, from COVID-19-related funding under ESSER III and ARP IDEA. Interdistrict revenue shows no significant change. The deck notes that Section 11t and Section 31o allocations are expected but are not included in this amendment.

Expenditure adjustments. Salaries increase about $1.7 million, or 2.2 percent, reflecting current staffing and lane adjustments, revisions to Schedule B and C contracts, and paraprofessional and non-represented wage adjustments ratified after the original budget was adopted. Benefits increase about $3.1 million, or 5.7 percent, driven by FICA and retirement costs tied to the salary changes plus a $2.3 million increase in MPSERS UAAL (unfunded accrued actuarial liability) retirement costs. Purchased Services increase about $323,000, largely from higher third-party substitute usage and rates. Payments to Other Districts increase about $459,000 for VLAC tuition. Supplies and Capital Outlay show no significant change.

The presentation frames the district's structural challenges under a 'So What, Now What' slide listing declining enrollment, federal funding, a structural deficit, strategic use of fund balance, and right-sizing staff. The budget schedule lays out the year's calendar: amend the 2021-22 General Fund again (Amendment #2) in March; amend the 2021-22 ancillary fund budgets in April; develop 2022-23 budgets and 2021-22 final amendments from April through May; and, in June, hold the public hearing and millage-rate adoption followed by adoption of the 2022-23 budget and the final 2021-22 budget amendment. The deck closes with a questions slide. Presenter figures are attributed to the Business Services department under Assistant Superintendent Rick West.

Following a November 9 workshop, the transportation department modeled reducing ridership eligibility distances by 0.25 and 0.5 miles, cutting eligible riders from 6,995 to 2,675 or 2,072 and reducing required drivers — but requiring elementary and middle school children to cross major roads, which administration does not recommend. The memo stresses an acute driver shortage, 13 short under the current five-tier system, rising to 35 under three tiers.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: A business-services memorandum (Rick West to Superintendent Rich Machesky, December 2, 2021) responding to the Board's November 9 workshop request to keep exploring a three-tier transportation model for modified school start times in 2022-23.

Eligibility scenarios modeled (walk distance to school):
- Current: 1.5 mi (HS/MS), 1.0 mi (Elementary) — 6,995 eligible riders
- +0.25 mi: 1.75 mi (HS/MS), 1.25 mi (Elem) — 2,675 riders
- +0.5 mi: 2.0 mi (HS/MS), 1.5 mi (Elem) — 2,072 riders

Buses needed for a 3-tier system:
- Current eligibility: 48 general-ed + 27 special-ed = 75
- +0.25 mi: 30 + 27 = 57
- +0.5 mi: 22 + 27 = 49

Key findings:
- The 0.25-mile change cuts eligible ridership ~62% and drivers by 18-20; the 0.5-mile change cuts ~70% and drivers by 26-28.
- Both changes would force elementary/middle students to cross major roads; administration does not recommend them.
- Tier comparison at current eligibility: 5-tier = 55 buses, 4-tier = 67, 3-tier = 75.

Staffing concern: District is short 13 drivers for the current 5-tier operation, a gap that grows to 35 under a 3-tier plan. Contingency would cancel general-ed routes equitably (sparing special-ed routes).

Other options raised: keep the 5-tier system but change the HS-MS-Elementary cadence, or eliminate high school transportation.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum on the Business Office letterhead (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; phone 248.823.4022) from Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, to Superintendent of Schools Rich Machesky, dated December 2, 2021, addressing the feasibility of a three-tier bus transportation system to support modified school start times for the 2022-23 school year.

Background: At the November 9, 2021 Board of Education workshop, after discussion of the challenges of a three-tier system, the Board asked administration to keep brainstorming solutions and signaled willingness to review the policy governing transportation eligibility. In response, the transportation department analyzed a three-tier model under two reduced-eligibility scenarios: decreasing the qualifying walk distance by 0.25 miles and by 0.5 miles. Under the 0.25-mile reduction, middle and high school eligibility falls to students living at least 1.75 miles from their building and elementary students at least 1.25 miles; under the 0.5-mile reduction, the thresholds become 2.0 miles (MS/HS) and 1.5 miles (elementary). The current thresholds are 1.5 miles (HS/MS) and 1.0 mile (elementary). For the analysis, the restriction against making students cross major roads was removed, because keeping it would leave eligibility at the current distances.

Eligible general-education riders by scenario: Currently 2,218 high school, 2,038 middle school, and 2,739 elementary students qualify (6,995 total). Under the 1.75/1.25-mile thresholds this drops to 1,130 HS, 547 MS, and 998 elementary (2,675 total); under 2.0/1.5-mile thresholds, to 911 HS, 428 MS, and 733 elementary (2,072 total).

Buses required for a three-tier system (excluding spares): current eligibility needs 48 general-ed and 27 special-ed buses (75 total); the 0.25-mile increase needs 30 general-ed plus 27 special-ed (57); the 0.5-mile increase needs 22 plus 27 (49). West notes the 0.25-mile change reduces eligible ridership by 62% and required drivers by 18-20, while the 0.5-mile change reduces ridership by 70% and drivers by 26-28. Both, however, would require elementary and middle school walkers to cross major roads, which administration does not recommend as a viable option.

For comparison at current eligibility, the memo tabulates bus needs by tier structure: the current five-tier system uses 32 general-ed and 23 special-ed buses (55 total); a four-tier system 40 plus 27 (67); and a three-tier system 48 plus 27 (75).

Staffing is the central concern. The district is currently short 13 drivers for its five-tier operation, and the shortage would grow to 35 under a three-tier system — figures that include the 8 standby drivers required for five tiers and 10 for three tiers. The shortage already forces the dispatcher, contract manager, and district manager to drive routes, and two additional retirements were prompting the combining of two to three routes the following week. Asked how a short-staffed three-tier system would be managed, West says the district would cancel routes in an equitable manner, excluding special-education routes — for example, canceling 25 of the 48 general-education routes on a routine basis if 25 drivers short — with significant operational impact. The memo closes by listing other options for modifying start times: maintaining the five-tier system while changing the HS-MS-elementary cadence, or eliminating high school transportation altogether.

The detailed bid tabulation and contract-award recommendation from the Barton Malow Company are attached.

Carson recommends the following vendors based on low qualified bidder: category 080000 Exterior Doors/Windows to Environmental Glass Inc. for $567,000.00; category 122413 Roller Shades to Triangle Window Fashions, Inc. for $13,540.00; a Strategic Change Order to Environmental Glass Inc. for $70,000.00; and an 8% contingency of $46,443.00, for a total recommended award of $696,983.00. All proposals were reviewed and qualified by the Bond Team of TMP Associates, Lecole Planners, and Barton Malow, and Environmental Glass has successfully performed similar work in neighboring school districts. A purchase order will be issued upon approval, with funding from the Building Site & Sinking Fund. The memo is copied to the Purchasing Department file, with attachments including the Bid Summary and Barton Malow Contract Award Recommendation, and supports agenda item 8.B at the December 14, 2021 regular Board of Education meeting.
